lesson.title: Dreams, demons and closure

steps.headline: A sceptical hypothesis says things seem as they do but are not.

lead.text: Descartes's example is an all-powerful deceiver, a demon. Dreams show that the senses can fool us. The demon could fool us about much more.
Yet to be deceived at all, Descartes must exist.
The modern sceptic turns the demon into a short argument. Test its shape as you would any argument: look for a case where both premises hold and the conclusion fails.

reveal.text: You tested the shape. The form is modus tollens, which has no counterexample row, so the argument is valid. A reply has to reject a premise.

I do not know I am not deceived by a demon.

conclusion.text: I do not know I have hands.

steps.headline: In 1939 G. E. Moore held up his hands. How can his argument and the sceptic's both be valid?

workedSteps.text: Both share a first premise: if I know I have hands, I know I am not deceived.
The sceptic starts from “I do not know I am not deceived”. Moore starts from “I know I have hands”.
Each reaches the opposite conclusion. Moore found his hands more certain than any philosophical premise against them.
Premise 1: if I know I have hands, I know I am not deceived.
Premise 2: I know I have hands.
Name the rule that takes these to “I know I am not deceived”.

lead.text: Test the sceptic's form with a truth table. The premise ¬q keeps only the rows where q is false. Then check which of those rows keep p → q true.

reveal.text: Only the row with p and q both false keeps both premises true, and there ¬p is true. Testing every row is how “this looks valid” becomes “this is valid”.

lead.text: Dretske and Nozick accept that you know you have hands. They deny that you can know you are not a handless brain in a vat.
Ask which general principle about knowledge those two verdicts contradict.

reveal.text: That principle is closure: if you know p, and know that p entails q, you know q. The sceptic's first premise is an instance of it. Their price: knowing you have hands without being able to know you are not envatted.

lesson.orientation: Reconstruct the sceptic's closure argument, test it, and compare the replies of Moore, Dretske and Nozick.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Your friend argues: “If you really know the shop is open, you know it hasn't burned down. You don't know that. So you don't really know it's open.”

intro.promise: By the end you'll test the sceptic's argument for validity and say which premise Moore, Dretske and Nozick each reject.
intro.whyItMatters: A valid argument can only be answered by rejecting a premise. That is how philosophers reply to scepticism.

recap.keyIdea: The sceptic's argument is valid, so it can only be answered by rejecting a premise. Moore trusts his hands over the premise. Dretske and Nozick give up closure.

blocks.text: You tested the sceptic's form row by row and ran the same premise backwards as Moore did. Then you saw which principle Dretske and Nozick reject.

recap.nextHook: Doubt comes in degrees. Next, how evidence should change how confident you are.

questions.prompt: Premises: 'If I know I have hands, I know I am not deceived by a demon' and 'I do not know I am not deceived by a demon'. Conclusion: 'I do not know I have hands'. Valid or invalid?
hints: Write it as p → q, ¬q, so ¬p.
Is there a row in which both premises are true and ¬p is false?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Valid. The form is modus tollens: p → q, ¬q, so ¬p.

questions.onCorrect: Valid: the form p → q, ¬q, so ¬p is modus tollens, and it has no counterexample row.

misconceptions.feedback: Look for a row where both premises are true and the conclusion false. Does one exist?

questions.prompt: Which philosopher answered the sceptic in 1939 by holding up his hands and arguing from 'here is one hand' to the existence of an external world?
hints: He was a Cambridge philosopher famous for defending common sense.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: G. E. Moore, in 'Proof of an External World'.

questions.onCorrect: G. E. Moore, in “Proof of an External World”: he trusted his hands over the sceptic's premise.

misconceptions.feedback: That philosopher belongs to another part of the story. The 1939 reply with raised hands came from a Cambridge champion of common sense.

questions.prompt: For the form 'p → q, ¬q, so ¬p', in how many of the four truth-table rows are both premises true?
hints: The premise ¬q keeps only the rows in which q is false.
In those rows, check where p → q is true.
A conditional with a true antecedent and false consequent is false.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only the row with p false and q false. There ¬p is true, so the form has no counterexample.

questions.onCorrect: One row keeps both premises true, and ¬p holds in it. The form has no counterexample.

misconceptions.feedback: The premise ¬q rules out the rows where q is true. Check which of the rest keep p → q true.
¬q removes every row where q is true. Count only what remains.

questions.prompt: Dretske and Nozick hold that you know you have hands but cannot know you are not a handless brain in a vat. Which principle about knowledge must they reject?
hints: Their two verdicts together contradict a general principle linking known claims to what they entail.
The principle says knowledge is 'closed' under known entailment.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Closure: the principle that knowledge carries over to what you know your knowledge entails.

questions.onCorrect: Closure: knowledge carries over to what you know your knowledge entails.

misconceptions.feedback: Think of a principle linking what you know to what it entails, not a rule of logic.

questions.prompt: What does Descartes' all-powerful deceiver, a deceiving God or evil demon, put in doubt that his dream argument leaves standing?
hints: Ask which beliefs would stay true even inside a dream.

acceptedIdeas: Simple truths of arithmetic, such as two and three making five
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Descartes notes that two and three make five whether he wakes or sleeps. An all-powerful deceiver could make him err even there.

choices.label: Simple truths of arithmetic, such as two and three making five

questions.onCorrect: Even awake or asleep, two and three make five. A demon could falsify such truths too.

misconceptions.feedback: Dreams already put such beliefs in doubt. Ask what would stay true even inside a dream.

questions.prompt: In the Second Meditation, what did Descartes take to survive even the demon's deception? Answer in two words.
hints: Even a deceiver needs someone to deceive.
The claim concerns the thinker himself.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'I exist': whatever deception he suffers, he must exist to be deceived.

questions.onCorrect: “I exist”: to be deceived at all, he must exist.

misconceptions.feedback: A deceiver could fake all of that. Ask what Descartes must be in order to be deceived.

questions.prompt: If the friend's two claims are true, must the conclusion be true? Answer yes or no.
hints: Try to imagine both claims being true while the conclusion fails.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes. The conclusion follows from the two claims, whether or not they are true.

questions.onCorrect: The shape guarantees the conclusion. Whether the claims are true is a separate question.

misconceptions.feedback: Try it. Suppose you know the shop is open, and you do not know it is unburned. Can both hold?

questions.prompt: Which rule of inference takes p → q and p to q? Answer with its Latin name.
hints: It is the rule that affirms the first part of an “if … then”.
questions.onCorrect: Modus ponens: from “if p then q” and p, infer q. It has no counterexample row.

misconceptions.feedback: Modus tollens starts from the denial of the second part. Here the second premise affirms the first part.

questions.prompt: Why can Moore's argument and the sceptic's both be valid?

acceptedIdeas: They start from opposite premises, so the dispute is over which premise to trust.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They start from opposite premises, so the dispute is over which premise to trust.

choices.label: They start from opposite premises, so the dispute is over which premise to trust.
One of them must be invalid.
Validity is a matter of opinion.

questions.onCorrect: Validity only says the conclusion follows. The quarrel is over which starting point deserves more confidence.

misconceptions.feedback: Both have valid forms. Compare where each one starts.
Validity is settled by the shape. The disagreement is about which premise to accept.

questions.prompt: “If I know I have hands, I know I am not a handless brain in a vat. I know I have hands. So I know I am not a handless brain in a vat.” Valid or invalid?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Valid: it has the form p → q, p, so q.

questions.onCorrect: Valid: the form p → q, p, so q has no counterexample row.

misconceptions.feedback: Look for a row where both premises are true and the conclusion false. Does one exist?
